title: Synthesis across sources
examples: How can I show that two articles disagree on a point?
What is the best way to blend ideas from different texts?
When I combine sources, do I need to say which source said what?

explain.say: Today we are learning to synthesize across sources. This means combining ideas from different texts. You will learn to weave them together smoothly.
First, you must identify key points in each source. Look for the main argument or piece of evidence. Each source has its own unique focus.

draw.text: Identify key points in each source

explain.say: Next, look for areas of agreement between the sources. Do both texts support the same idea? You can use words like similarly or likewise.
Then, you must look for tension or contradiction. Do the sources offer opposing views? You can use words like however or conversely to show this.
For an everyday example, consider two news reports on a storm. One might focus on the high winds, and the other might focus on the resulting power outages.
A common mistake is summarizing each source separately. This just lists information instead of combining it. You need to build a new argument.

items: Do not just summarize Source A, then Source B.
Instead, weave them into one cohesive argument.

faq.q: How do I transition smoothly when I combine two ideas?
faq.a: Use transition words like furthermore, moreover, or similarly. These words help guide the reader through your combined thought.
asks: What linking words should I use?
How do I make my writing flow better?

faq.q: If the sources disagree, should I pick a side?
faq.a: You should present the tension fairly. Explain both sides and then offer your own reasoned conclusion based on the evidence.
asks: Is it okay to disagree with the sources?
How do I show conflict between texts?

faq.q: What is the difference between summarizing and synthesizing?
faq.a: Summarizing retells what the sources said. Synthesizing creates a new insight by combining those separate points.
asks: Does synthesis mean I have to agree with everything?
Is synthesis just putting two summaries together?

faq.q: Do I need to mention the source every time I use an idea?
faq.a: It depends on your essay's requirements. Generally, you integrate the evidence and cite the source when you first introduce the idea.
asks: When do I need to mention the author?
How much do I need to cite?

faq.q: Can I synthesize sources about different topics?
faq.a: Yes, if the underlying concept connects them. For example, comparing economic impacts across different historical periods.
asks: What is a common thread between sources?

facts: Synthesis involves creating a new understanding from existing parts.
Identifying agreement shows how sources reinforce a point.
Noticing tension highlights complexity or debate on a topic.
Effective synthesis moves beyond simple summary.

quiz.say: Source A says the policy helped workers, and Source B says it hurt small businesses. What is the best approach?
quiz.show: A: Good for workers; B: Bad for business

options.show: Presenting both claims and analyzing the trade-off between them.
options.say: Presenting both claims and analyzing the trade-off between them.

options.show: Saying the sources are both wrong.
options.say: Saying the sources are both wrong.

quiz.why: This shows you can handle conflicting evidence thoughtfully.

wrong.1: This ignores the evidence provided by Source B.
wrong.2: This misses a key opportunity to analyze the sources deeply.
wrong.3: You must engage with the evidence given, even if you critique it later.

quiz.say: If Source A and Source B both discuss the rise of trade, and both mention increased global travel, what should you do?
quiz.show: Both sources mention increased global travel

options.show: Writing two separate sentences about travel.
options.say: Writing two separate sentences about travel.

options.show: Focusing only on the travel aspect.
options.say: Focusing only on the travel aspect.

options.show: Claiming one source is more correct about travel.
options.say: Claiming one source is more correct about travel.

options.show: State that both sources corroborate the idea of increased global travel.
options.say: State that both sources corroborate the idea of increased global travel.

quiz.why: Using words like 'both' or 'similarly' confirms agreement.

wrong.0: This is just listing; it does not synthesize the shared idea.
wrong.1: You might be missing other unique points from the sources.
wrong.2: You should report the evidence, not judge its overall truthfulness.

quiz.say: Which technique is most crucial when you want to show that two historical accounts contradict each other?

options.show: Using only commas to separate the opposing ideas.
options.say: Using only commas to separate the opposing ideas.

options.show: Repeating the opposing ideas in the same paragraph.
options.say: Repeating the opposing ideas in the same paragraph.

options.show: Simply putting the two source quotes back-to-back.
options.say: Simply putting the two source quotes back-to-back.

options.show: Using contrasting transition words like 'however' or 'conversely'.
options.say: Using contrasting transition words like 'however' or 'conversely'.

quiz.why: These words signal a shift in argument, showing tension clearly.

wrong.0: Commas are too weak; they do not signal a major shift in argument.
wrong.1: This creates repetition rather than a focused analysis of the conflict.
wrong.2: This lacks your analysis to explain why the contradiction matters.
